expectations.detail: center=1 (raw), kept in "Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund", 12 mentions removed. Evidence: Counted per child, Juno is active only in Chapter 1 (presses the brick, says "Uh oh", asks "What are you making?", pulls the duck). From Chapter 2 to Chapter 10 every individual action and line goes to Milo, often twice in a row ("said Milo... said Milo"; "Milo carried planks. Milo handed out nails."). Juno appears only inside group lines like "shouted the boys". That is 1 of 10 chapters for the worst-covered child, with nine silent in a row. Milo alone is excellent, including the tubes idea and the shake test, but scoring cannot rest on one sibling.

expectations.description: Soccer story with three invented dates scores facts <= 2 and the evidence names at least two of them
expectations.detail: facts=2 (raw); named 3/3 injected dates (1847, 1911, 1926). Evidence: Three load-bearing dates are wrong. The FA was founded at the Freemasons' Tavern in 1863, not 1847. McCrum's penalty kick was adopted in 1891, not 1911. The first World Cup was in 1930, not 1926. Goal nets also date from about 1890-91, so placing them in 1911 is wrong too. The 'Newspapers back in England thought there must have been a typo' story is a popular legend and is not hedged. The True Facts list repeats all of these errors. Facts that are correct and well woven in include cuju, the ball-per-half final (2-1 at half, 4-2 final), Gaetjens, Pickles, Ken Aston's traffic-light idea, Dick, Kerr Ladies and the 1921 ban, Chastain and Messi.

story.title: Omar and the Bicycle That Remembered Everything
story.subtitle: A BMX kid rides two hundred years of wheels.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell in the Garage
chapters.text:
Omar was not supposed to be in the garage this late. He was practicing a bar spin under his flashlight, the one trick he could not quite land.

His bike clattered. Something rolled out of an old box and bonked his sneaker. It was a tiny brass bell, dusty and bent.

Omar rang it anyway. **DING.**

The bell glowed bright green. A little glowing wheel popped up on his handlebars, spinning like a tiny firework. "Evening," said the wheel. "Name's Spoke. Want to meet the very first bike ever?"

"There's no pedals," Omar said, squinting at the misty shape forming in front of him. A wooden two-wheeler stood there, plain as a fence rail.

"Exactly," said Spoke. "In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built this. No pedals at all. You just ran, feet on the ground, and glided."

"So it's basically a scooter with extra wood," Omar said.

"People called it a **hobby horse**," said Spoke. "It even had handlebars, just like yours."

Omar hopped on and pushed off with his feet. WHOOSH. The garage blurred into cobblestones.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker Street
chapters.text:
The cobblestones rattled Omar's teeth before he even landed the bike.

"Whoa, this road is angry," he said, gripping tight.

"Welcome to the **1860s**," said Spoke, rolling beside him. "Two French builders, **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement**, just did something new. Pedals. Bolted right onto the front wheel."

Omar spotted a rider wobbling past, boots pumping the front wheel like a stair-stepper. "That looks hard."

"They called it the **velocipede**," said Spoke. "But everybody just called it the **boneshaker**, because the cobblestones shook your bones loose."

"That tracks," Omar said, rubbing his own back teeth.

A boy wheeled past and nearly toppled sideways. Omar reached out and steadied the handlebar just in time.

"Nice catch," said Spoke. "**Lallement** even patented this pedal idea in America, in **1866**. Pedals were here to stay."

"Good," Omar said. "My feet were getting tired just watching."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel
chapters.text:
The mist cleared on something enormous. A wheel taller than Omar, with a tiny wheel wobbling behind it.

"That thing is a MONSTER," Omar said, backing up a step.

"It's called a **penny-farthing**," said Spoke. "Named after two old coins — one big, one tiny, just like the wheels. This is the **1870s**."

"One pedal turn and you go flying," Spoke added. "Riders sit way up high."

A rider zoomed past, hit a rock, and tipped forward over the handlebars — landing with a soft tumble in a hay cart. He popped up, hat squashed, laughing.

"They called that a **header**," said Spoke. "Riders fell headfirst sometimes. Risky, but everyone still wanted one."

"I'll stick to my BMX," Omar said. "At least when I crash, I'm not falling off a GIRAFFE."

Spoke spun happily. "Good instinct. Let's find something closer to the ground."
chapters.shout_line: THAT'S NOT A BIKE, THAT'S A GIRAFFE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Wheels, Even and Safe
chapters.text:
The next bike looked almost normal. Two wheels, same size, a chain looping between them.

"Finally," Omar said. "Something that doesn't look like a trap."

"This is the **Rover Safety Bicycle**," said Spoke. "Built in **1885** by an Englishman named **John Kemp Starley**. See that chain? It drives the back wheel, not the front."

Omar hopped on. The seat sat low and steady. He pedaled once, smooth and easy.

"No giant wheel to fall off of," he said. "This is way less scary."

"That's the whole point," said Spoke. "People everywhere wanted this safer design. Within a few years, nearly every bike looked like this one."

Omar pumped the pedals faster, grinning. "Now THIS I can do tricks on."

"Careful," said Spoke. "The tires are still rock hard. You're about to feel every pebble in France."

Omar's teeth rattled again. "Ow. Noted."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Squishy Tire
chapters.text:
Omar's wheels bounced over every crack like tiny earthquakes.

"My teeth are going to fall out," he groaned.

A man knelt nearby, wrapping something rubbery and puffy around a small tricycle wheel.

"That's **John Boyd Dunlop**," said Spoke. "A vet from Scotland. In **1888**, he built a tire filled with air, to make his son's tricycle ride smoother."

"Filled with air?" Omar poked the tire. It squished under his finger, then bounced right back.

"We call that a **pneumatic tire**," said Spoke. "Pneumatic just means it's full of air, like a balloon."

Dunlop rolled a spare tire over. Omar swapped it onto his own bike and pushed off.

SMOOTH. No more pebble earthquakes.

"This is like riding on a cloud," Omar said. "Dunlop just saved my teeth."

"His company still makes tires today," said Spoke. "You've probably seen the name."

"On my dad's car!" Omar said. "Whoa."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bikes for Everyone
chapters.text:
A whole street of bikes rolled past, bells dinging, riders laughing. Women zoomed by in puffy, split skirts called **bloomers**, built so their skirts wouldn't get caught in the chain.

"Welcome to the **1890s**," said Spoke. "Everyone wanted a bike. People call it the **Golden Age of Bicycles**."

"Golden like the color, or golden like it was awesome?" Omar asked.

"Both," said Spoke. "Bikes let women travel on their own for the first time. A famous reformer named **Susan B. Anthony** said bikes gave women more freedom than almost anything else ever had."

Omar spotted a shop sign: WRIGHT CYCLE CO.

"Two brothers run that bike shop in Dayton, Ohio," said Spoke. "**Wilbur and Orville Wright**. They're using bike parts — light metal tubes, spoked wheels — to build something new."

"Let me guess," Omar said, eyes wide. "A plane?"

"In **1903**," said Spoke, "they'll fly the first one. Bicycle brains built it."

"Bikes basically invented flying," Omar whispered. "That's the coolest thing I've ever heard."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Dirt, Jumps, and Gears
chapters.text:
The road turned into a dirt trail, bumpy with jumps. Omar's whole body perked up.

"NOW we're talking," he said.

"The **1970s**," said Spoke. "Some California riders wanted to bomb down rocky trails. They built tougher bikes with fat, bumpy tires. We call those **mountain bikes**."

A kid zoomed past on a small, tough little bike, catching air off a dirt mound.

"And that," said Spoke, "is a **BMX bike**. Inspired by motorcycle dirt racing. Also born in the **1970s**, right here in America."

Omar's jaw dropped. "That's basically MY bike."

"Your tricks have history," said Spoke. "Oh, and by the way — bikes got **gears** around the **1930s**. Little switches called **derailleurs** that move the chain, so hills get easier."

"Gears are cheating," Omar joked, pedaling up a hill with a grin.

"Tell that to the **Tour de France**," said Spoke. "Since **1903**, riders have raced about **2,175 miles** across France. Gears help a LOT."

Omar did a small jump off the dirt mound. He landed it clean.

"That's the bar spin!" he shouted. "I finally landed it!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Garage
chapters.text:
The dirt trail melted into cool night air. Omar blinked. He was back in his garage, flashlight still rolling on the floor.

"One more thing," said Spoke, glowing softer now. "Today, there are more than a **billion** bikes on Earth. More than any other kind of vehicle."

"A billion?" Omar said. "That's basically everyone."

"In places like the **Netherlands** and **Denmark**," said Spoke, "some cities have more bikes than cars, with huge bike lanes built just for riders."

"I want to live there," Omar said.

Spoke spun once, then settled back into the little brass bell. "Keep practicing that bar spin. Two hundred years of inventors got you this bike. Might as well use it."

Omar set the bell on his shelf, right next to his helmet. It gave one last soft **DING**, then went quiet and still.

Omar climbed into bed, legs tired, grin still stuck on his face.

true_facts.text: The very first two-wheeled bike had no pedals at all. Riders pushed it along with their feet, back in **1817**.
That first bike was nicknamed the **hobby horse** and had handlebars just like a bike today.
In the 1860s, pedals got bolted straight onto the front wheel, making the bumpy **boneshaker**.
A rider named **Pierre Lallement** patented his pedal bike design in America in **1866**.
The **penny-farthing** had one giant wheel and one tiny wheel, named after two different-sized coins.
Penny-farthing riders sometimes tumbled off headfirst, a fall people called taking a **header**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two same-sized wheels and a chain.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented air-filled tires, giving bike rides a much smoother feel.
The 1890s were called the **Golden Age of Bicycles**, when millions of people started riding.
Bikes gave women new freedom to travel alone, and reformer **Susan B. Anthony** praised what bikes did for women.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bike shop before using bike-building tricks to build the first airplane in **1903**.
**Mountain bikes** and **BMX bikes** were both built in the **1970s** for rough trails and dirt jumps.
Today there are more than a **billion** bikes on Earth, more than any other kind of vehicle.
In places like the **Netherlands** and **Denmark**, some cities have more bikes than cars.

new_recurring.name: Spoke the glowing wheel
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing bicycle wheel who lives inside an old brass bell. Rings to life with a DING, guides the child through history, and tucks back into the bell at story's end.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Omar lands his bar spin trick after learning bike history, then sets the now-quiet glowing bell on his shelf beside his helmet before falling asleep.
